<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S5" title="In ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5 </span>The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S5.SS1" title="In 5 The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5.1 </span>Scaling with Data</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" title="In 5.1 Scaling with Data ‣ 5 The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">ECHO’s advantage persists with more pretraining data.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S5.SS2" title="In 5 The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5.2 </span>Scaling with Depth</span></a>

</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S5.SS3" title="In 5 The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5.3 </span>Stability across Runs</span></a>

</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">
<span id="id2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">

</span></span></div>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.24766v1/teaser_stage_pairs_ZCR.svg" id="S1.F1.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/359;" width="476" height="359"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Benchmark gain by task class over the fourteen benchmarks of
<a href="#A3.T1" title="In Appendix C Full Benchmark Results ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#A6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix F After Supervised Finetuning ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, each panel against the DeepSeek baseline of
its own stage. ECHO-1.5<sup id="S1.F1.sf1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S1.F1.sf1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(3)</span></sup> matches ECHO-3’s gain at half its MTP overhead.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.24766v1/intro_al7_ZCR.svg" id="S1.F1.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/544;" width="476" height="544"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Accepted length against serving depth <math id="S1.F1.sf2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, filled inside the trained depth
and hollow beyond it. ECHO keeps gaining where auxiliary MTP saturates.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Multi-horizon supervision on the backbone’s own final layer buys downstream performance after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning (a) and drafting depth beyond what was
trained (b).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs)
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>
are predominantly trained with the
<em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Next-Token Prediction</em> (NTP) objective.
While NTP has demonstrated remarkable scalability and effectiveness,
it provides supervision only at the immediate next-token horizon,
leaving potentially useful future information unexploited.
Moreover, autoregressive decoding remains inherently sequential,
resulting in limited inference throughput.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To better utilize future information,
recent work has explored <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Multi-Token Prediction</em> (MTP)
as an auxiliary objective on top of NTP.
By introducing additional future-token prediction targets,
MTP provides denser supervision during training and can generate draft tokens for speculative decoding, enabling inference acceleration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Early MTP methods predict multiple future positions independently from the same hidden state <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gloeckle et al. (2024)</a></cite>, providing denser supervision but ignoring causal dependencies among future tokens. Subsequent causal MTP methods such as DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a></cite> address this limitation by introducing autoregressive dependencies among future prediction steps, significantly improving prediction quality and improving the backbone model’s overall performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blakeman et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al. (2026)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, both causal and parallel MTP remain auxiliary by construction: future-token prediction is carried out by dedicated modules attached to the backbone, rather than being integrated into the autoregressive generation process itself. This leads to two limitations:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Indirect Multi-Horizon Supervision</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MTP losses primarily supervise the auxiliary prediction modules.
Consequently, the backbone model receives multi-horizon learning signals only indirectly, potentially limiting their impact on long-horizon planning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Costly Long-Horizon Supervision</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Denser supervision requires deeper prediction horizons, yet each additional horizon adds a prediction module in memory and another pass in compute.
This cost limits the prediction horizon in large-scale causal MTP pretraining, typically to a single draft token.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address the above limitations, we introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO)</span>, a causal self-recursive
framework that reuses the backbone’s final layer for future prediction and
samples per-step prediction depths with decaying probabilities to reduce the amortized MTP training overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Final-layer parameter sharing</em> ensures that multi-horizon losses directly shape the backbone, rather than being absorbed by horizon-specific auxiliary modules.
As shown in <a href="#S3.F3.sf1" title="In Figure 3 ‣ Sharing promotes longer-horizon supervision. ‣ 3.1 Direct Multi-Horizon Supervision via Final-Layer Sharing ‣ 3 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a>, this allows ECHO to benefit from deeper supervision: its downstream performance continues to improve at depth 3, whereas DeepSeek’s MTP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> does not, consistent with observations in MiMo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLM-Core Xiaomi, 2025</a>)</cite>.
More fundamentally, training the same parameters responsible for next-token generation to predict multiple future tokens encourages the backbone to anticipate how the sequence unfolds over subsequent steps, as evidenced by ECHO’s substantial gains on reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To make long-horizon supervision computationally efficient, we introduce <em id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS)</em>, which samples prediction depths with decaying probabilities. This simultaneously reduces the amortized MTP training overhead and mitigates the impact of increasing prediction errors and supervision noise at greater depths. After supervised finetuning, ECHO’s advantage grows further.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beyond its pretraining benefits, ECHO entirely eliminates the need for post-hoc drafter finetuning</span>. DDS makes longer-horizon supervision affordable, while final-layer parameter sharing enables depth extrapolation: since the same shared layer is reused at every draft step, ECHO can extend drafting beyond the trained prediction depth while maintaining high acceptance rates, at an amortized MTP training overhead of only 1.5 depth-1 steps (see <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Training Shallow, Drafting Deep ‣ 4 Pushing the Frontier of Speculative Decoding under Realistic Serving ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). By drafting directly with its pretrained weights, ECHO avoids the overfitting to academic benchmarks associated with post-hoc drafter finetuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, yielding substantial acceptance-length gains in realistic, high-entropy generation settings as shown in <a href="#S3.F3.sf2" title="In Figure 3 ‣ Sharing promotes longer-horizon supervision. ‣ 3.1 Direct Multi-Horizon Supervision via Final-Layer Sharing ‣ 3 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(b)</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO)</span>, which predicts every future horizon by recursively applying the backbone’s own final layer, with the per-step prediction depth drawn from a distribution decaying along depth.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ECHO imposes direct multi-horizon supervision, beating auxiliary MTP on reasoning and code at matched depth while holding on QA &amp; multiple choice, and widening its lead on both classes after supervised finetuning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ECHO makes long-horizon prediction cheap in compute and free in parameters, and keeps gaining acceptance when extrapolating in depth, where auxiliary MTP saturates. It eliminates drafter finetuning entirely, yet outperforms post-hoc drafters, especially on open-ended generation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Multi-Token Prediction</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) augments next-token prediction with future-token targets, improving language modeling while providing draft tokens for speculative decoding. It inherits the architecture of speculative draft models and differs in the training regime: draft models are finetuned post-hoc against a frozen backbone on a limited dataset, whereas MTP modules are optimized jointly with the backbone throughout pretraining.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Parallel MTP predicts multiple future positions independently from several output heads on a shared backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gloeckle et al. (2024)</a></cite>, following Medusa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Causal MTP instead follows EAGLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024)</a></cite>: DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a></cite> feeds dedicated prediction modules the previous hidden state together with shifted token embeddings, preserving autoregressive dependencies among future steps, and GLM-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al. (2026)</a></cite> shares those parameters across all depths, as EAGLE does, to reduce memory cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Post-hoc Drafter</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Post-hoc drafters are trained on top of a frozen target model by finetuning on target-generated responses, and differ mainly in how a block of draft tokens is produced.
Medusa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al. (2024)</a></cite> attaches parallel heads that draft every position from the final hidden state, while EAGLE-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2025)</a></cite> re-enters a lightweight decoder once per drafted token, conditioned on target hidden states, preserving token-to-token dependency.
Recent parallel drafters build on DFlash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2026)</a></cite>, which predicts the whole block in one pass, with DSpark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al. (2026)</a></cite> restoring intra-block dependency through a lightweight causal head.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Two limitations are nonetheless inherent to post-hoc drafting.
First, the drafter is narrowly aligned with the target, being finetuned on a dataset orders of magnitude smaller than the pretraining corpus.
Second, scaling that training to the pretraining corpus is compute-heavy from the multi-step or multi-layer overhead, which has not been shown to improve the backbone’s downstream performance and may even degrade training.
ECHO overcomes both: joint pretraining aligns it with the target, and its supervision improves the backbone at modest overhead.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Looped Transformers</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers across iterations, buying computational depth without new parameters: parameter efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, adaptive computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dehghani et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, reasoning at LLM scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saunshi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, test-time compute scaling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and depth allocated per token <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bae et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In all of them recursion refines the same token position under a next-token objective; ECHO instead recurses along the horizon, each step conditioning on the next future token to predict one position further ahead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Yet both buy structure rather than recall, and for looping that is a trade: at matched parameters and compute it leads on reasoning but trails on perplexity and closed-book QA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saunshi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and at scale its gain is credited to knowledge manipulation rather than capacity, measured against external dense families rather than a same-recipe baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. ECHO pays no such price: mathematics, reasoning and code gain while multiple choice and closed-book QA hold (<a href="#S3.F3.sf1" title="In Figure 3 ‣ Sharing promotes longer-horizon supervision. ‣ 3.1 Direct Multi-Horizon Supervision via Final-Layer Sharing ‣ 3 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a>), and both classes gain after finetuning (<a href="#S4.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Staying Aligned under realistic setting ‣ 4 Pushing the Frontier of Speculative Decoding under Realistic Serving ‣ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion BeyondAuxiliary Multi-Token Prediction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a>). Looping, latent chain-of-thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and ECHO thus price latent computation differently: repeated passes over one position, annotated chains, and extra positions — the one price that accepted tokens can repay.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
